slides.teaching: Tell students this studio produces exactly four files/artifacts named on the last slide - work toward those, not toward extra polish.

slides.title: Recall Monday's vocabulary before you start
rows: a table of Series sharing one index
a function that belongs to an object, called with a dot
a value named at the call site
a short description inside triple quotes, right under def
slides.callout: Every term here came from Monday's lecture - if one feels shaky, flag it before Studio 1, not after.
slides.teaching: Cold-call one student per row to give the architectural example before moving to the studio cycle.

slides.title: The interview, as one sequence
slides.alt: Flow diagram of five boxes - shape, .dtypes, .head(), .info(), .isna() - leading to a final box reading only now: filter, derive, export.
slides.caption: Five questions, in order, before any cleaning decision is made.
slides.explainBody: Each box is one question with one call that answers it. The point is not the five method names - it is that all five come BEFORE the box at the bottom. Filtering or deriving a column first means deciding without evidence.
slides.teaching: Walk the five boxes out loud, then cover the bottom box and ask what would go wrong if a student started there. Every studio slip this week is a version of skipping to the bottom box.

slides.title: Repeat one studio cycle for every exercise

steps.label: PREDICT
steps.head: Write the expected result
steps.body: Include shape, dtype, or expected count.

steps.label: RUN
steps.head: Execute one cell
steps.body: Use Ctrl+Enter and leave later cells untouched.

steps.label: INSPECT
steps.head: Read the evidence
steps.body: Check Console output and Variable Explorer state.

steps.label: EXPLAIN
steps.head: Interpret the result
steps.body: State what the result means and one limitation.

slides.teaching: Same cycle as Weeks 2-3 - name it, do not re-teach it.

slides.title: Confirm your folder, then load Radley Hall
slides.code:
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

print(Path.cwd())

DATA_PATH = Path('data') / 'building_rooms.csv'
rooms = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH, sep=',')
print(rooms.shape)
slides.explainHead: Same ritual as Weeks 1-3, one new keyword argument
slides.explainBody: Path.cwd() and the working-folder check are the same habit from Week 1B. sep=',' is the keyword argument from Monday's lecture - explicit here because a comma-separated file is what this course always uses, but naming it removes any doubt for someone reading your script later.
slides.teaching: Path.cwd() will differ by machine; only rooms.shape has one correct answer everyone should match: (24, 12).

slides.title: Studio 1: load the dataset and confirm its scale
slides.prompt: Before touching a single value, know how big the table is.
steps: Run cells [0]-[1] and read the printed shape.
Predict rows and columns before printing shape.
Confirm 24 rooms, 12 recorded columns.
Find rooms in the Variable Explorer and open it.
slides.teaching: If a student's shape differs from (24, 12), check DATA_PATH before anything else - a wrong file, not a wrong idea, is the likely cause.

slides.title: Commit to a dtype before you print it
slides.code:
# R303 has no recorded has_daylight value
print(rooms['has_daylight'].dtype)
slides.question: What dtype does this print?
slides.why: A bool array cannot hold a missing value. R303's missing entry forces the whole has_daylight column to fall back to dtype object.
slides.teaching: Take a show of hands before revealing - most students guess bool. This previews the answer-key table on the very next slide.

slides.title: The trustworthiness interview - your answer key
rows: one missing value (R303) breaks the bool dtype
slides.callout: This table summarizes dtypes + isna().sum() side by side - it is NOT the literal text info() prints (the real printout follows Studio 2). If your own numbers don't match, stop and find the difference before continuing.
slides.teaching: This is the same real, verified pandas 3.0.5 output from Monday's lecture - not a simplification. Students check their own console against it line by line.

slides.title: Studio 2: run the interview yourself
slides.prompt: dtypes, head, info, and isna().sum() - all four, on your own machine.
steps: Print rooms.dtypes and find the one object column.
Print rooms.head() and rooms.info().
Print rooms.isna().sum() and name both missing values by room_id.
Compare your output with the answer key - do not skip a mismatch.
slides.teaching: Circulate and check that students can name which room_id is missing which value, not just that a count is 1.

slides.title: Commit to what info() hands back
slides.question: What does the second line print?
slides.why: info() prints its summary as a side effect and returns nothing. x holds None, so print(x) prints the word None, not the summary again.
slides.teaching: Connect back to Week 3's def/return lecture - a function that prints but never returns produces None, exactly like info() here.

slides.title: Check your info() output against the real thing
slides.output:
<class 'pandas.DataFrame'>
RangeIndex: 24 entries, 0 to 23
Data columns (total 12 columns):
 #   Column            Non-Null Count  Dtype  
---  ------            --------------  -----  
...
 6   has_daylight      23 non-null     object 
 7   energy_kwh_m2_yr  23 non-null     float64
...
dtypes: float64(6), int64(1), object(1), str(4)
memory usage: 2.4+ KB
slides.explainBody: This is the exact, verified pandas 3.0.5 output for rooms.info() - not a simplification, and not the same thing as the hand-built dtype answer-key table from before Studio 2. If your own printout doesn't show has_daylight and energy_kwh_m2_yr both at 23 non-null, stop and find the difference before Studio 3.
slides.teaching: Point out info() returns None - the predict slide just before this one rehearses exactly that. A good moment to contrast print-as-side-effect with a method that returns a value.

slides.title: A data dictionary and a provenance note, recalled

left.head: Data dictionary
left.body: One entry per column: name, unit or allowed values, meaning. Write it before trusting a single number - Project 1 requires one for every dataset you submit, including your own later.

right.head: Provenance note
right.body: Where the file came from, when, and under what assumptions - one or two sentences is enough. For Radley Hall: instructor-built, fictional, for this course only.

slides.teaching: Ask a student to state Radley Hall's provenance note from memory before revealing the next slide.

slides.title: Radley Hall's data dictionary - the reference you'll extend
rows: building half the room sits in
room has at least one exterior daylight opening
slides.callout: Fictional, instructor-built data for this course - not a real building. Say this in your own provenance note whenever data isn't yours.
slides.teaching: This excerpt covers 4 of 12 columns; Studio 3 asks students to write all twelve in their own script.

slides.title: Studio 3: write your data dictionary and provenance note
slides.prompt: Extend the reference table above to all 12 columns, in your own script.
steps: List every column, its unit or values, and its meaning.
State where Radley Hall's data came from (see the reference slide).
Note which two values are missing, by room_id.
Save both as Python strings or comments in your script.
slides.teaching: A dictionary entry that just repeats the column name ('area_m2: the area in m2') is incomplete - require unit AND meaning AND, where relevant, allowed values.

slides.title: NaN marks a value nobody recorded, recalled
slides.definition: Recall from Monday: pandas' marker for a missing value - not zero, not an empty string, not False. A genuine absence, in any column type.

example.head: Two real gaps in Radley Hall
example.body: R303 has no recorded has_daylight value; R206 has no recorded energy_kwh_m2_yr. rooms.isna().sum() reports exactly one NaN in each column - finding gaps like these, before trusting a single number, is the whole point of the trustworthiness interview.

slides.note: NaN is contagious in arithmetic: 5 + NaN is NaN, not 5. Derive a column from one with a gap, and that row silently becomes NaN too.
slides.teaching: Ask: is an empty string the same as NaN? No - isna() only flags true gaps, not deliberately-recorded empty text.

slides.title: NaN as a modeling decision, recalled

left.head: Drop the row
left.body: Removes a record entirely - defensible when the missing value is required for the analysis at hand, e.g. you cannot compute an energy comparison without energy_kwh_m2_yr.

right.head: Keep the column, flag the gap
right.body: Dropping has_daylight would throw away 23 good values to fix 1 gap. Keep it, but remember its dtype (object) and count (23/24) every time you use it.

slides.teaching: Ask why 'drop the column' and 'drop the row' are not the only two options - flagging-and-keeping is the one beginners forget.

slides.title: Read the filter line one part at a time

parts.label: DataFrame
parts.body: The loaded table - one row per room.

parts.label: Column selector
parts.body: Brackets + a quoted name pull out one Series.

parts.label: Method call
parts.body: True where a value IS recorded, False where it's NaN - one Boolean per row.

slides.teaching: This is the exact line the next two slides use - predict its result first, then confirm against the real code.

slides.title: Commit to a row count before you filter
slides.code:
# only R206 lacks a recorded energy_kwh_m2_yr
mask = rooms['energy_kwh_m2_yr'].notna()
cleaned = rooms[mask]
print(cleaned.shape)
slides.question: What does the last line print?
slides.why: The mask keeps rows with a recorded value: 23 of 24, 12 columns untouched. (1,12) inverts it; (23,11) confuses row vs. column drops.
slides.teaching: A student who answers (1, 12) has isna()/notna() backwards - worth a direct correction before Studio 4.

slides.title: One drop, one keep - both documented
slides.explainBody: Filtering to notna() rows drops room R206 (its only fault: no energy reading) and keeps everything else, including R303's still-missing has_daylight value, which we keep and flag rather than drop. One drop, one keep, both documented - this week's central judgment call.
slides.teaching: Verified against pandas 3.0.5: Copy-on-Write means skipping .copy() here would not corrupt rooms or raise a warning, unlike what older tutorials claim - .copy() is still required for explicit, readable intent (see the definition slide right after this one).

slides.title: .copy() makes cleaned independent of rooms
slides.definition: A DataFrame method that returns an independent copy of the data. The moment .copy() runs, the copy and the original become two separate objects in memory - editing one never edits the other.

example.head: cleaned = rooms[mask].copy()
example.body: rooms[mask] already returns a new, filtered table in pandas 3.0 - editing it does not corrupt rooms. Adding .copy() anyway is this course's required habit: it states your intent in the code itself, so anyone reading the script later knows cleaned stands on its own.

slides.note: Older tutorials warn skipping .copy() raises a SettingWithCopyWarning. Verified: pandas 3.0's Copy-on-Write removed that warning here.
slides.teaching: This corrects a real, verified pandas 3.0 behavior change - do not teach the old SettingWithCopyWarning as if it still fires.

slides.title: Studio 4: build the cleaned subset and justify it
slides.prompt: Every dropped row or column needs one written sentence.
steps: Filter to rows with a recorded energy_kwh_m2_yr.
Confirm the result is 23 rows, and name the dropped room_id.
Write one sentence justifying the drop.
Write one sentence justifying why has_daylight stays, unfixed.
slides.teaching: The two justification sentences are graded content, not filler - a cleaned file with no written reasoning behind it fails Project 1's Part I rubric line later.

slides.title: One vectorized column, in one small documented function
slides.explainHead: Same vectorized idea as Monday's NumPy slide - now a documented function
slides.explainBody: np.array(area_m2) turns the column into a NumPy array; * 10.7639 converts every room's area at once - no loop, no per-row copy-paste. Wrapping it as convert_m2_to_ft2, with a docstring and a type hint on the parameter and return value, is this week's required 'one clean function per pipeline stage' - the same convention from Monday's lecture, now applied to real data. The next slide adds a second function.
slides.teaching: Ask why we didn't just write cleaned['area_m2'] * 10.7639 without wrapping it in np.array - both work here; the np.array wrapper makes the NumPy connection explicit for teaching, not because pandas needs it.

slides.title: ...continued: a second documented function
slides.explainHead: Intensity and total answer different questions
slides.explainBody: energy_kwh_m2_yr is an intensity (per square meter); energy_kwh_yr is a real total. R306, the Server closet, has the highest intensity in the whole building - 410 kWh/m2/yr - but at only 8.0 m2 that multiplies into a modest 3,280 kWh/yr, well below several ordinary Studios. Two functions, two documented pipeline stages, one dataset.
slides.teaching: Ask which column answers 'how efficient is this room per square meter' and which answers 'how much energy does this room actually use in a year' - Studio 5 sorts by neither yet (that is Week 5), but does compare the two directly on the student's own dataset.

slides.title: Export the cleaned dataset - keyword argument again
slides.explainBody: Without index=False, pandas writes its own row-number column into the file - clutter nobody asked for (Monday's slide on to_csv). This is the exact line Project 1 requires for every CSV you submit.
slides.teaching: Confirm (23, 14): 23 rows survived the energy-based filter, 14 columns because area_ft2 AND energy_kwh_yr were both added on the two previous slides. Forgetting index=False would add a stray Unnamed: 0 column instead, making it (23, 15).

slides.title: Studio 5: add the column, then export
slides.prompt: Turn cleaned into one shareable file.
steps: Add area_ft2 with a single vectorized line.
Confirm the dtype is float64, not object.
Export with cleaned.to_csv(path, index=False).
Reopen the exported file and confirm its shape.
slides.teaching: Check that students reopened the exported CSV to confirm it, rather than trusting the write silently succeeded.

slides.title: What your scatter should roughly show
slides.chartTitle: area_ft2 vs. energy_kwh_m2_yr - Radley Hall (23 rooms)
slides.explainHead: Read the shape, not just the code
slides.explainBody: Each point is one room; color marks zone. Most points sit under 100 kWh/m2/yr, except one server closet far above the rest. We'll name that formally as an outlier next week - for now, just notice it.
slides.teaching: This chart is built from the same cleaned, verified numbers your own script will produce - it is a target to compare against, not a substitute for running your own plt.scatter.

slides.title: Studio 6: build your own Matplotlib scatter
slides.prompt: One static figure: area_ft2 (x) against energy_kwh_m2_yr (y).
steps: plt.scatter(cleaned['area_ft2'], cleaned['energy_kwh_m2_yr'])
Label both axes with their units.
Add a title naming the building and room count.
Save the figure with plt.savefig(...) and open the file.
slides.teaching: Students should notice the same high outlier point the reference chart showed - if they don't see it, their cleaned subset likely dropped the wrong row.

slides.title: Studio 7: self-check on a different room
slides.prompt: Prove your pipeline generalizes past the one room you traced live.
steps: Pick room R204, not R101 - a room you haven't hand-checked yet.
Assert its area_ft2 equals round(area_m2 * 10.7639, 1).
Assert cleaned has zero missing energy values.
Assert has_daylight still shows exactly one missing value.
slides.teaching: This is the required weekly transfer check: 2-4 self-written assert statements on an input different from the one worked through live. Expected: R204 area_ft2 = 699.7.

slides.title: Studio 8: audit an AI-generated cleaning script
slides.prompt: AI drops rows with dropna(), overwrites area_m2, and skips index=False.
steps: Find the factual error in the AI's own comment.
Identify which two rooms dropna() silently removes.
Explain why overwriting area_m2 destroys provenance.
Add index=False and record every accepted, modified, and rejected change.
slides.teaching: Expected findings: the comment claiming has_daylight is 'already a clean bool column' is false; dropna() removes R303 and R206 for two unrelated reasons; overwriting area_m2 leaves a m2-named column holding ft2 values; the missing index=False adds a stray Unnamed: 0 column.

slides.title: This studio previews Project 1, Part I
slides.statement: Interview, document, clean, derive, export - the exact five moves Project 1 Part I will ask you to repeat on a dataset you choose yourself.
slides.supporting: Project 1 opens this week (dataset selection); nothing here is graded twice - today's Radley Hall practice is what makes next week's version, on your own data, faster.
slides.teaching: Remind students dataset selection for Project 1 opens now, separate from tonight's submission - Radley Hall stays the shared in-class example through Week 7.

slides.title: Submit one small, honest evidence package

steps.label: DICTIONARY
steps.head: Data dictionary + provenance
steps.body: Every column, unit, meaning, and source.

steps.label: MEMO
steps.head: Drop-justification memo
steps.body: One sentence per dropped row or column - or per kept-but-flagged one.

steps.label: FIGURE
steps.head: NumPy + Matplotlib touch
steps.body: area_ft2 column and its scatter plot, saved as an image.

slides.teaching: All four artifacts come from one script - there is no second file this week.

slides.title: Exit check: defend one decision
slides.prompt: Pick one cleaning decision - a drop, or a keep-and-flag.
steps: State the decision in one sentence.
Name the evidence that justified it.
Name what it does NOT prove.
Be ready to explain it cold, no notes.
slides.teaching: Cold-call two volunteers. This rehearses the kind of question a Project 1 pin-up will ask in Week 8.

slides.title: Trustworthy data is documented, not just clean
takeaways: Interview every dataset before you trust it: shape, dtypes, head, info, NaN.
Every drop and every kept gap needs one written sentence.
A vectorized NumPy column and a Matplotlib scatter took five lines, not a loop.
This exact workflow is Project 1, Part I - on your own data, starting now.
slides.teaching: Students save, restart the kernel, run from the top, and submit the script plus its exported CSV and figure before Monday, 9:00am.
